source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating pipeline parallelism. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers across stages and can require microbatching to reduce pipeline bubbles.
corrected_answer: Runbook: pin model, precision, stage map, topology, schedule, microbatch count, software, workload lengths, concurrency, and a matched baseline. Verify stage placement, activation/communication/KV-cache memory budgets, and output correctness; warm up, then repeat randomized trials across load and lengths. Mechanism: stages exchange activations and overlap independent microbatches, but dependencies, transfers, and fill/drain create waits and buffers. Measure per-stage compute/transfer/wait, utilization, queueing, TTFT, decode p50/p95/p99, throughput/goodput, peak memory, errors/OOMs, and correctness. Boundary: gains at saturated throughput may disappear for low load, short requests, imbalanced stages, slow links, or tail latency.
risks: Aggregate throughput can hide stage imbalance, queueing, tail-latency regressions, or failed requests.
Activation buffers and serving state can exceed weight-only memory estimates.
evidence_required: Versioned model/runtime, topology, partition, schedule, microbatching, workload, concurrency, and matched baseline.
Repeated phase-aware measurements with stage traces, latency distributions, memory high-water marks, failures, and output checks.

source_user: Define MoE and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model has multiple expert subnetworks and a router that selects a top-k subset for each token; only selected experts execute for that token, reducing active feed-forward compute relative to running every expert. Mechanism: the router dispatches token representations across devices, experts process them, and outputs are gathered and combined, often requiring all-to-all communication. Boundary: lower active FLOPs does not guarantee lower latency or cost—routing imbalance, token-capacity overflow, communication bandwidth, expert replication, and small batches can dominate. Measure router load balance, dropped/overflow tokens, communication time, per-expert utilization, memory, latency, throughput, and output quality on the target topology.
risks: Top-k, capacity-factor, auxiliary-loss, routing precision, and implementation details change behavior.
Expert imbalance or all-to-all contention can erase active-compute savings and harm tail latency or quality.
evidence_required: Model/router top-k and capacity policy, expert placement, topology, precision, batch/length distribution, and dense baseline.
Per-expert token counts, overflow/drop rate, communication traces, memory, latency/throughput, and quality checks.

source_user: Define MoE and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: MoE replaces a single dense feed-forward block with multiple experts plus a learned router. For each token, the router chooses (for example) top-1 or top-2 experts, so active computation can scale with selected experts rather than the total parameter count. Mechanism: token dispatch and combine move activations between devices when experts are sharded, creating all-to-all traffic and synchronization. Boundary: parameter capacity and active compute are different; an MoE may fit or compute less yet be slower or less reliable when routing is imbalanced, capacity is exceeded, or links are congested. Validate with fixed routing policy and matched dense measurements of communication, expert load, overflow, memory, latency, throughput, and quality.
risks: The claimed benefit depends on top-k, capacity factor, load balance, and hardware/software implementation.
Dropped or rerouted tokens can affect output quality, not just performance.
evidence_required: Router policy, capacity/overflow behavior, expert placement and topology, precision, workload, and matched dense baseline.
Expert utilization and token accounting, communication time, memory, latency/throughput distributions, failures, and quality evaluation.

source_user: Define MoE and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: A Mixture-of-Experts layer contains several alternative feed-forward experts and a router; each token is sent to a selected subset, commonly top-1 or top-2. This can provide many total parameters while executing fewer expert blocks per token. Mechanism: dispatch scatters token activations to expert ranks and a combine step restores token order, so distributed MoE adds communication and synchronization. Boundary: active-FLOP reduction is not a universal latency or cost reduction; skewed routing, capacity overflow, small batches, and limited interconnect bandwidth can dominate. Measure per-expert load, overflow/drops, dispatch/combine time, compute, memory, latency percentiles, throughput, and task quality.
risks: Different routing and overflow policies can change both performance and quality.
Mean utilization can hide hot experts, communication bottlenecks, and tail latency.
evidence_required: Top-k and capacity policy, placement/topology, implementation, precision, workload, and comparison baseline.
Router and expert telemetry, communication traces, memory high-water marks, latency/throughput tails, failures, and quality checks.

source_user: Define MoE and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: MoE uses a router to assign each token to a small number of expert feed-forward networks instead of executing one shared feed-forward network for every token. The infrastructure reason it matters is that total model capacity can grow without proportional per-token expert compute, but serving becomes a communication and scheduling problem. Mechanism: distributed dispatch sends tokens to expert owners and combine returns their weighted outputs. Boundary: this advantage assumes balanced routing and adequate capacity/bandwidth; overflow, expert hotspots, or low batch reuse can increase drops, memory, latency, or cost. Report router load, overflow, communication, compute, memory, latency/throughput, and quality against a matched dense reference.
risks: Total parameter count must not be confused with active parameter count or deployed memory.
Capacity and routing choices may trade quality against utilization and tail latency.
evidence_required: Expert count, top-k, capacity factor, overflow policy, placement, interconnect, precision, and dense reference.
Repeated workload measurements including expert load, drops, communication, memory, latency percentiles, throughput, and quality.

source_user: Define MoE and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: A Mixture-of-Experts model has a learned router and multiple expert blocks; for each token, only a selected top-k set of experts contributes, while the remaining experts are inactive for that token. Mechanism: token dispatch and return of weighted expert outputs require routing metadata, activation movement, and synchronization, especially when experts reside on different devices. Boundary: fewer active experts does not by itself establish faster or cheaper serving—imbalanced assignments, capacity drops, all-to-all traffic, memory replication, and request length/load can reverse the benefit. Use a matched dense baseline and collect expert-load histograms, overflow, communication/compute time, memory, latency tails, throughput, errors, and quality.
risks: Router and capacity behavior can vary by token distribution and batch composition.
Quality regressions from dropped or poorly routed tokens may be missed by performance-only tests.
evidence_required: Routing/top-k, capacity and overflow policy, expert placement, topology, workload, and dense baseline.
Token-level routing and quality checks plus repeated communication, memory, latency, throughput, and failure measurements.

source_user: Contrast MoE with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: A naive dense implementation applies the same feed-forward block to every token, with predictable local execution but compute and parameter capacity tied to that block. MoE instead routes each token to selected experts, allowing larger total capacity with fewer expert blocks active per token. Mechanism: distributed MoE scatters activations to expert owners and gathers results, adding routing and all-to-all communication that the dense path may avoid. Boundary: MoE is not automatically faster or cheaper; imbalance, overflow/dropped tokens, communication contention, or small batches can outweigh reduced active compute. Compare matched model quality, precision, hardware, workload, and software while measuring expert load, communication, memory, latency tails, throughput, failures, and output correctness.
risks: A dense baseline with different parameter count or quality is not an attributable comparison.
MoE routing can introduce drops, hotspots, or communication-induced tail latency.
evidence_required: Matched model/quality target, precision, device topology, routing and capacity policy, batch/length/load, and implementation.
Per-expert load and overflow, communication traces, memory, latency distributions, throughput, errors, and output/quality checks.

source_user: Contrast MoE with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: The naive dense design runs one shared feed-forward computation for every token; MoE has multiple experts and activates only a router-selected subset. MoE can increase total parameter capacity without executing all experts per token, whereas dense execution avoids expert dispatch and generally has simpler memory and scheduling behavior. Mechanism: when experts are distributed, token activations move through scatter/all-to-all and gather/combine operations before the next layer. Boundary: compare only with controlled workloads and an appropriate quality/parameter baseline: an MoE speedup may vanish under low batch, skewed routing, capacity overflow, or constrained links. Measure phase latency percentiles, throughput, memory, communication, expert utilization, drops, failures, and quality.
risks: Parameter-count, active-FLOP, and memory comparisons answer different questions.
Routing skew and all-to-all congestion can produce tail regressions hidden by averages.
evidence_required: Explicit dense comparator, model/quality target, top-k/capacity policy, topology, precision, workload, and software versions.
Repeated per-expert and phase-aware telemetry, overflow/drop and correctness checks, memory, latency, throughput, and failure data.

source_user: Contrast MoE with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: In a dense baseline, every token uses the same feed-forward weights. In MoE, a router selects top-k experts per token, so the model may have larger total capacity while activating fewer expert blocks. Mechanism: token-to-expert dispatch and output combination require scatter/gather and, across devices, all-to-all communication and synchronization; the dense path has no equivalent expert routing step. Boundary: active-compute savings are workload- and topology-dependent and can be lost to imbalanced experts, overflow, communication, or memory replication. Run matched tests and report router load, dropped tokens, communication/compute time, memory, latency p50/p95/p99, throughput, failures, and quality.
risks: Dense and MoE systems may differ in quality, total parameters, and memory footprint, confounding claims.
Token distribution changes routing balance and can alter results substantially.
evidence_required: Matched comparator definition, routing/capacity settings, placement/topology, precision, workload lengths and load.
Expert-level routing, overflow, communication, memory, latency/throughput, failure, and quality measurements over repeated trials.

source_user: Contrast MoE with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: A naive dense model sends every token through one shared feed-forward block, while an MoE model routes each token to a small subset of specialized experts. The MoE trade-off is higher total capacity with potentially lower active compute versus extra routing and distributed-systems complexity. Mechanism: dispatch scatters token activations to expert devices and combine gathers their weighted outputs, with synchronization at the routing boundaries. Boundary: do not infer an MoE win from FLOP counts alone; capacity overflow, hot experts, small batches, interconnect limits, memory, or tail latency can make it worse than dense. Use matched baselines and measure expert load/overflow, communication, compute, memory, latency distributions, throughput, failures, and quality.
risks: Routing policy and capacity factor couple performance to token distribution and may affect quality.
A dense comparator with unequal quality or hardware allocation can invalidate the contrast.
evidence_required: Dense comparator and quality target, expert/router settings, capacity/overflow handling, topology, precision, workload, and load.
Repeated expert-load and communication traces, memory high-water marks, latency tails, throughput, failures, correctness, and quality results.
